explanations.explanation: Altars it is, friend. Hosea says, “The more his fruit increased, the more he increased the altars.” The fruit went up and the altar count went right up with it. When my cookie orders go up, I buy more flour. When Israel's fruit went up, Israel increased the altars.

Wells is a sensible guess, since a thriving vine wants water. But Hosea never mentions wells here. He says, “The more his fruit increased, the more he increased the altars.” Altars is the word he uses.
Towers is a fair guess, friend. But that's not what Hosea says. He says, “The more his fruit increased, the more he increased the altars.” The word he uses is altars.
True. Hosea says, “The better his land produced, the better he made the sacred pillars.” The land got an upgrade, and so did the pillars. Good catch, baker.

It's easy to doubt a line that sounds backwards, friend. But Hosea really says, “The better his land produced, the better he made the sacred pillars.” So a better harvest led to better pillars. Nothing in the verse says they got worse, and nothing says they got ignored.

Right. Hosea says, “The LORD will break down their altars and demolish their sacred pillars.” These are the altars and pillars from verse 1, where Israel increased the altars and made the pillars better. Now the LORD says He will take them down. Two strong verbs in one line: break down, demolish.

Israel might have hoped for that, friend. But Hosea says the opposite: “The LORD will break down their altars and demolish their sacred pillars.” The altars Israel kept adding don't stay standing. They come down.

Verse 1 might make that sound likely, friend. There, the altars increased and the pillars were made better. But the LORD says the opposite. Hosea says, “The LORD will break down their altars and demolish their sacred pillars.”

explanations.answer: We do not revere the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, and it comes out of their own mouths. Hosea says they will say, “We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD.” Then they ask, “What can a king do for us?” I think that's a people admitting something out loud.

explanations.answer: The LORD has not sent one
explanations.explanation: That one sounds reasonable, but it isn't what the people say. Hosea says they will say, “We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD.” The reason they give is about themselves, not about the LORD holding something back. They point at their own lack of reverence.

explanations.answer: We do not honor our elders
explanations.explanation: Elders never come up in this verse, friend. The people give a different reason. Hosea says they will say, “We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD.” It's all about the LORD.

I can see why that sounds right, since kings usually do a lot. But look at what the people actually say: “What can a king do for us?” That's a question, and it sounds to me like they expect the answer to be nothing. So the statement is False.

False, friend. The people don't say a king can do a lot. They say, “What can a king do for us?” I think that question shows a people who've run out of hope in their king. The verse leaves it at the question.

Weeds. Hosea says, “So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field.” A furrow is where a farmer plants something good, and here the thing coming up is poison. Anybody who's pulled weeds out of a garden knows how fast they take over. False oaths go in, judgment comes up.

Flowers would be a lovely surprise in a field, friend. But Hosea doesn't give that kind of surprise. He says, “So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field.” Poisonous weeds, not flowers, come up in those furrows.

Grain is exactly what a farmer hopes to see in those furrows. That's what makes Hosea's line sting. He says, “So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field.” Furrows that should hold grain hold poison instead.

explanations.answer: It has been taken into exile
explanations.explanation: That's it. Hosea says the people and its idolatrous priests will mourn over it, “…for it has been taken from them into exile.” The priests who rejoiced in its glory are the ones grieving. The calf doesn't stay where they left it.

explanations.answer: It has been melted in a fire
explanations.explanation: Fire is a dramatic idea, but Hosea doesn't mention it. What he says is that the calf “…has been taken from them into exile.” It isn't destroyed in this verse. It's carried away.

explanations.answer: It has been smashed by a prophet
explanations.explanation: A prophet doing the smashing is a fair guess, friend. But this verse has nobody smashing anything. It says the calf “…has been taken from them into exile.” The mourning is over something carried away.

Assyria, friend. Hosea says, “Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king.” The calf of Beth-aven is the one whose glory its priests rejoiced in. Now it's carried off to Assyria as tribute.
Egypt is a famous name in the Bible, so I get why it jumped out. But Hosea names a different place. He says, “Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king.”
Babylon is a name a lot of people know, friend. But it isn't the one in this verse. Hosea says, “Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king.” Assyria is the place named.

I can see why that might sound right, but the king doesn't stay behind. Hosea says, “Samaria will be carried off with her king like a twig on the surface of the water.” The king goes right along with her. So the statement is False.
False, friend. Hosea says, “Samaria will be carried off with her king like a twig on the surface of the water.” The king is carried off with her. That makes the statement False.
Covered up, friend. Hosea says they will say to the mountains, “Cover us!” and to the hills, “Fall on us!” I think that's a heavy thing to say. It sounds like people who want to disappear.
Lifted up is the opposite of what Hosea says. The people ask the mountains, “Cover us!” and the hills, “Fall on us!” They aren't asking to go higher. I think it's a heavy moment.

That would be a calmer scene, friend, but it's not this one. Hosea says they will say to the mountains, “Cover us!” and to the hills, “Fall on us!” They aren't asking questions. They're asking to be covered.

That would be a happy ending, friend, but it isn't what Hosea says. He says, “Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained.” Israel didn't leave the sin behind. They stayed in it. So the statement is False.
False. Hosea says, “Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained.” They didn't leave the sin behind. That's a long stretch of staying put.
The battle. Hosea asks, “Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?” He asks it as a question about the battle in Gibeah. That battle is what overtook the sons of iniquity.
A famine is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. Hosea asks, “Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?” The thing that overtook them was a battle.
Plague is a scary word, but it's not the one Hosea uses. He asks, “Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?” What overtook them at Gibeah was a battle.

Nations, friend. The LORD says, “I will chasten them when I please; nations will be gathered against them to put them in bondage for their double transgression.” Other nations, gathered together against Israel. That's the group in the verse.
Angels are all over the Bible, so I get the guess. But this verse has a different group. It says, “nations will be gathered against them to put them in bondage for their double transgression.”
Prophets are a fair guess, friend. But they aren't the ones gathered here. The verse says, “nations will be gathered against them to put them in bondage for their double transgression.”

A yoke, friend. The verse says, “…I will place a yoke on her fair neck.” A yoke is the wooden frame that hooks a working animal to its load. The heifer who loves to thresh is the one getting the yoke, and the LORD says, “I will harness Ephraim…”
A crown is a nice thought, friend. But the verse puts something else on her neck. It says, “…I will place a yoke on her fair neck.” A yoke is a harness, not a crown.
A garland is pretty, and I see why it fits a fair neck. But the verse doesn't mention flowers. It says, “…I will place a yoke on her fair neck.” That's a harness.

That's the work. Hosea says, “I will harness Ephraim, Judah will plow, and Jacob will break the hard ground.” Plowing and breaking hard ground are the jobs handed out. Notice it's all field work, no sitting around.

Gathering and storing grain is a real farm job, friend, but it isn't one listed here. Hosea says, “…Judah will plow, and Jacob will break the hard ground.” The work named is plowing and breaking ground.
Guarding and watering are real farm jobs, but they aren't the ones listed. Hosea says, “…Judah will plow, and Jacob will break the hard ground.” Plowing and breaking ground are the jobs in the verse.

explanations.answer: It is time to seek the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the why. Hosea says, “For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” The reason given for breaking up the unplowed ground is that it's time to seek the LORD. Nice work, baker.

That's a believable farm reason, friend, but it isn't the one Hosea gives. He says, “For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” The reason is about seeking the LORD, not about the harvest.

explanations.answer: The ground will soon be sold
explanations.explanation: A sale makes a tidy reason, but nobody sells anything in this verse. Hosea says, “For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” That's the reason given.
Rain. The verse ends with the LORD coming and sending righteousness upon them “like rain.” Rain is what a freshly broken field is waiting for. It's a picture of something coming down from above.
Fire is a strong picture, friend, but not the one in this verse. Hosea says the LORD “…comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” Rain is what he names.
Wind is a fair guess, since weather is the theme. But the verse says the LORD “…comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain.” After the plowing, the picture is rain.

explanations.answer: The multitude of their mighty men
explanations.explanation: That's it. Hosea says, “Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men…” So there's their own way, and then there's a big crowd of strong fighters. They counted on both.

Gold is a logical thing to trust in, friend, but the verse never mentions it. Hosea says they trusted “…in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men…” It's their own way and their fighters.

That sounds like it could fit, but Egypt isn't in this verse. Hosea says, “Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men…” The second thing they trusted was their many mighty men.
True. Hosea says the roar of battle will rise against the people, “…so that all your fortresses will be demolished…” All of them, not just a few. Nice work, baker.
It's hard to picture fortresses falling, friend, but that's what the verse says. Hosea says “…all your fortresses will be demolished…” So the statement is True. The word is all.

explanations.answer: He will be utterly cut off
explanations.explanation: Utterly cut off, friend. Hosea says, “When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off.” I think that's a serious line, so I'll let it stand.
Fleeing is a natural thing for a king to try, but this verse doesn't say it. Hosea says, “When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off.” There's no escape trip in the text.

explanations.answer: He will hide in the hills
explanations.explanation: Hiding in the hills sounds like a plan, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Hosea says, “When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off.” That's what happens to him.
